content:
Hi everyone,

I am very excited to share that I think I've completed formalizations of both Busch's theorem (2003, the POVM variant, and the corollary restricting to projections) and Gleason's Theorem: the original PVM version, for complex Hilbert spaces of finite dimension ≥ 3, in Lean4, including the classical dispersion-free (no hidden variables) corollary. To my knowledge, it hasn't been done yet.

theorem gleason {n : ℕ} (hn : 3 ≤ n) (m : ProjMeasure n) :
∃! ρ : H n →ₗ[ℂ] H n, IsDensityOperator ρ ∧
∀ A : Submodule ℂ (H n), m.μ A = bornValue ρ A

As an independent researcher without an academic affiliation, I've been working on this project for some time, and the proofs now fully check (0 project-specific axioms, 0 sorry). My math background is solid, but of course not deep enough in this particular corner of the literature to have pulled this off alone, and my Lean skills are pretty modest. So I leaned heavily on AI assistance to generate, debug, and structure the code, with every proof checked by the kernel along the way.

It took me a few tries to get here. The first attempts didn't pan out as standalone proofs, but they left me with good foundations, an architecture, and a clear plan to build on. Gleason was of course the harder of the two. The project works through frame functions and the continuity/density arguments on the unit sphere that the POVM version conveniently sidesteps, which meant building some intermediate results along the way that might be worth having in mathlib4 on their own.

You can find the repository and the source code here: https://github.com/Bobart0/gleason-theorem-lean
(tag v1.0.1-gleason), Apache 2.0

Since I am outside the traditional academic circuit, I'd immensely appreciate your feedback on the code quality, proof architecture, and style. Ultimately, I have two main goals:

  • I would love some guidance on how to properly clean this up and break it down into PRs to eventually contribute it to mathlib4.
  • I would welcome any advice (or potentially an endorsement) on how to publish a preprint of this work on arXiv as an independent author.

Thank you forward for your time and your insights!

Interesting!

This may be suitable for PhyslibAlpha, which fits topic-wise, and, as I understand it, will accept (but not maintain) AI contributions.

Trivial comment: non-English docstrings will reduce the number of people who will engage with the code.
